title: Burn vs SLO: Architecture & Budget Probe — Thalia Industries
summary: Initial technical/financial discovery focused on per-token burn vs latency SLOs for Thalia's customer-facing assistant. Discussed batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization, hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC tradeoffs. Agreed to run a 2-week perf pilot: 1M tokens/day baseline, measure P50/P95 latency and unit cost. Redwood to send pricing spreadsheet, security pack, and proposed pilot runbook.
topics: prefix/KV cache impact on unit economics
hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC tradeoffs
security and compliance (KMS, SOC2, audit logs)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Jordan (Head of ML, Thalia), Priya (Platform Eng), Liam (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you squeezing this in. Quick intro round, then we'll jump into your constraints — cost, latency, and what success looks like.
[00:10] Jordan: Cool, thanks. I'm Jordan, I run ML at Thalia. We're building a real-time customer assistant, about 1M messages a day today, expected to double. Latency is big for us.
[00:20] Liam: Yeah, hi. CTO here, main ask is predictable spend and no surprises on burst days.
[00:25] Priya: Platform team — we'll own networking/VPC and compliance hooks.
[00:30] Maya: Great. Ravi, want to frame the tradeoffs?
[00:34] Ravi: Sure. At a high level the levers we use to move unit cost are batching, prefix/K V caching, model selection/quantization, and routing between hosted and dedicated pools. Batching reduces per-token infra cost but can add a few ms to tail latency depending on your tolerance.
[00:50] Jordan: When you say batching, what's the typical cost delta we could expect? Numbers help.
[00:56] Ravi: From our experience, for chat workloads with variable prompt lengths, enabling continuous batching and aggressive coalescing can drop per-token infra cost by around 25–45%. If you add hot-prefix caching (client conversation history pinned) you can get another ~10–30% on top, because you avoid repeated compute for repeated context. But these are workload-dependent.
[01:20] Priya: Are those numbers assuming you host the model or we run Dedicated?
[01:25] Ravi: Good question. The percentages are at the runtime level and hold for both, but contract/pricing differences matter. Hosted gets you simple per-token billing; dedicated gives you a reserved capacity price — lower variable unit cost at scale but fixed monthly commitments.
[01:40] Liam: Our CFO threw out a hard ceiling: $8k/month for the assistant for the pilot phase. We can expand if we hit SLAs.
[01:48] Maya: Understood. Jordan, can you sketch your SLOs? P50/P95?
[01:53] Jordan: We want P50 < 70ms and P95 < 200ms for the generation step; whole request — including post processing — under 250ms. If that can't be met we need a fallback plan.
[02:05] Ravi: Ok, P95 200ms is tight for large models if you also expect high concurrency. Two obvious approaches: 1) smaller model + prompt engineering for latency-critical paths, or 2) Dedicated GPUs with pre-warmed KV caches and shorter CUDA kernels; both help lower tail.
[02:22] Jordan: Can hosted hit that?
[02:24] Ravi: It can, for many customers we hit ~120–180ms P95 on optimized flows with caching and batching tuned, but it depends on model size and prompt lengths. For the absolute lowest tail latency at scale, Dedicated with reserved GPU pools typically gives more predictable P95.
[02:40] Priya: What about private deployment? We have data residency and KMS requirements — keys must live in our cloud account.
[02:47] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and VPC peering; you retain key control and audit logs. There's an on-prem package too. Pricing for private includes platform licensing plus infra.
[02:58] Liam: So Private costs more upfront but gives compliance guarantees. Any tip on mixing Hosted and Private? Hybrid routing?
[03:06] Ravi: Yes, hybrid routing is common: burst and non-sensitive traffic to Hosted for cost efficiency, and sensitive PII traffic to Private. Also automatic fallback to smaller quantized model if capacity constrained.
[03:18] Jordan: Quick clarifying Q — when you say K V cache, are we talking prefix-only, or full KV for decoder states?
[03:24] Ravi: We do prefix-level caching plus KV cache reuse for short-lived sessions; the runtime maintains KV across the convo to avoid recomputing early layers. It's not a full transcript store but it reduces tokens reprocessed.
[03:36] Priya: Any privacy risks with caching? Can cache be encrypted with our keys?
[03:40] Ravi: Cache is encrypted at rest; for Private we can bring your KMS. For Hosted we encrypt with Redwood-managed keys but we do offer Bring-Your-Own-Key for some enterprise tiers. We'll send the security doc.
[03:51] Jordan: Let's talk numbers. If we assume 1M messages/day average token length 150 tokens per message — rough math — that's 150M tokens/day. Even with batching and caching that seems huge and would blow the budget.
[04:02] Maya: Ok that's a key discrepancy — 1M messages/day at 150 tokens is 150M tokens/day. Is that current actual or peak theoretical?
[04:10] Jordan: That's today in our logs for chat turns including system prompts. Sorry maybe my numbers are inflated — our active users are 100k/day with avg 10 messages each, maybe 1M isn't steady-state. We need the pilot to instrument real token burn.
[04:22] Ravi: Good, pilot will measure effective tokens after you apply truncation, system prompt trimming, and prefix caching. Typical effective tokens can be 30–60% lower than raw counts once prompt optimization and cache hits are in place.
[04:35] Liam: For budgeting, what's a realistic pilot scope that fits $8k/month?
[04:40] Maya: For $8k, assuming hosted per-token list pricing and some batch/caching uplift, you could run a focused pilot ingesting ~20–30M effective tokens over the month with targeted latency tuning. Dedicated would be hard to justify with that budget — reserved capacity typically starts at several tens of thousands per month.
[04:58] Jordan: We can narrow pilot to a 2-week POC for 1M effective tokens/day on a subset of users — maybe power-users only.
[05:05] Priya: On SLA, if we hit high latency, what's fallback?
[05:09] Ravi: Fallbacks we commonly use: model tiering (route to a faster smaller model), cached responses for repeated queries, and circuit-breaker to denylist heavy prompts. We can implement automatic routing rules in the console.
[05:21] Jordan: How much work is the routing rule setup? We prefer declarative rules.
[05:24] Ravi: It's declarative in the console — you define thresholds (latency or cost) and routing policies. We can pre-seed with recommended thresholds for your workload during the pilot.
[05:34] Priya: Security again — SSO and RBAC? We need role separation, audit trails.
[05:39] Maya: Redwood supports SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs with retention configurable for enterprise. We'll include the SOC2 and syslog/audit doc in the packet.
[05:49] Liam: How does quantization affect quality? We can't lose accuracy on some intents.
[05:54] Ravi: Quantization generally reduces model size and can slightly affect probability mass, which can show up as small changes in phrasing. For intent detection use-cases it's often negligible; for high-stakes generation we recommend dataset-level evals. We also do hybrid where we quantize for non-latency-critical flows and keep fp16 for critical ones.
[06:11] Jordan: Anything on warmup and cold-starts? P95 spikes on first requests are painful for us.
[06:15] Ravi: We pre-warm kernels and maintain hot KV caches for pinned sessions on Dedicated. Hosted has warm pools but at scale you can see cold starts on infrequent models; we can configure keep-alive policies for sessions in the pilot.
[06:27] Maya: Let's talk about measurable success criteria for the 2-week pilot. Jordan?
[06:31] Jordan: Measure P50 < 70ms, P95 < 200ms, effective token reduction >= 30% from prompt tuning + caching, and unit cost <= $0.0000X per effective token — we need to agree on exact per-token target after Redwood shares pricing.
[06:46] Ravi: We'll map scenarios. For example: mid-size model on Hosted with batching plus prefix cache — typical effective per-token cost X; Dedicated reserved pool for same throughput typically reduces variable cost by ~20% but adds fixed monthly. We'll send a worked example spreadsheet.
[07:05] Priya: On instrumentation, what telemetry do we need to measure effective tokens and cache hit rate?
[07:10] Ravi: We expose token-level metrics, cache hit rate, per-route latency histograms, and per-token cost breakdown. You can forward traces to your observability tool (Datadog/Prometheus).
[07:20] Jordan: Any gotchas around token counting differences? We use tiktoken-e-like counts; do you align with that?
[07:26] Ravi: We generally use the widely-adopted tokenizer counts and will align on your tooling. Slight mismatches can happen if system prompts are encoded differently; we'll normalize during pilot.
[07:36] Liam: If we do Dedicated, what's the commitment and how fast can you spin capacity?
[07:41] Maya: Dedicated starts at multi-week provisioning; we can do expedited setup for pilots on shared, reserved preemptible pools. Commit terms are monthly or annual, with discounts for longer terms. For small pilots we recommend Hosted with a dedicated routing lane to emulate Dedicated behavior.
[07:56] Priya: Do you support bring-your-own-GPU / on-prem?
[08:00] Ravi: Yes, through Redwood Private on-prem package; it's heavier operationally but meets strict residency and k8s isolation requirements.
[08:07] Jordan: Let's touch pricing coarse numbers now so we can ballpark. If you give per-token hosted price A and reserved dedicated price B, we can compute rough burn.
[08:16] Maya: I'll avoid exact list pricing on the call but we can say: hosted variable pricing tends to be higher per-token compared to dedicated amortized across a commit. For pilot we'd propose hosted bill plus a credit if you convert to Dedicated within 90 days.
[08:29] Jordan: Fair. We need the spreadsheet.
[08:31] Maya: Action for us: share a worked pricing/spreadsheet and a pilot runbook with recommended batching and cache settings.
[08:39] Ravi: Also want to flag model recommendations — if you need extreme P95 we might propose a smaller low-latency model for fallback and a mid-size for quality-critical flows.
[08:49] Priya: About telemetry retention — we need logs for 90 days and audit trails for a year. Can Redwood support that?
[08:56] Maya: Yes, enterprise retention add-on covers longer retention and compliance exports. We'll include options.
[09:03] Jordan: Do you have examples where customers achieved >30% effective token reduction? Curious on tactics.
[09:08] Ravi: Yes — two levers: 1) system prompt consolidation and dynamic truncation; 2) prefix caching for repeated context (e.g., customer profile pieces). In one retail case we saw a 42% reduction after trimming system prompts and enabling cache.
[09:23] Liam: I worry about the human cost of ops — who configures thresholds and monitors burn?
[09:28] Maya: We partner on runbooks; your SREs do day-to-day but Redwood SEs will support initial config and tuning during the pilot. We can also propose a short managed runway as an add-on.
[09:38] Priya: Networking: will VPC peering add latency?
[09:42] Ravi: Peering itself is negligible; cross-account NACLs and routing can add ms if misconfigured. With Private, colocating in the same region and AZ reduces latency.
[09:52] Jordan: Ok, sales/ops checks — our procurement needs a price sheet and SOC2 + encryption docs to start legal.
[09:58] Maya: We'll send pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 report, KMS and network architecture notes, and a proposed 2-week pilot runbook.
[10:05] Liam: Timeline expectations? We want pilot next month if possible.
[10:09] Maya: We can start onboarding in two weeks pending signatures and a brief prep call.
[10:14] Jordan: One more technical: how do you measure cache hit rate for partially matching prefixes?
[10:19] Ravi: We track exact and fuzzy prefix hit metrics, plus token-level savings per hit. We'll provide dashboards in the console and prometheus export.
[10:29] Priya: Anything on model drift monitoring? We need quality alerts if outputs degrade after quantization.
[10:35] Ravi: Redwood Optimize can run evals against saved prompt sets and raise regression alerts; part of pilot we can configure baseline evals and alert thresholds.
[10:44] Jordan: Okay let's recap next steps.
[10:48] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pricing spreadsheet, security package (SOC2, KMS, VPC notes), pilot runbook with configured batching/cache defaults, and an initial perf checklist. Thalia to confirm pilot subset users and internal contacts.
[10:59] Priya: I'll confirm the networking contacts and share our SAML metadata.
[11:03] Liam: I'll loop in procurement for contract timeline.
[11:06] Jordan: We'll aim to kick off the pilot in ~2 weeks.
[11:10] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and a short prep doc.

[End of transcript — note: transcript has intermittent mis-attributions and automatic captions may have minor inaccuracies]
